planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost into shallow, well-drained, alkaline or caliche-based soil; this dwarf coneflower needs excellent drainage and struggles in heavy, wet clay.

directions: A diminutive, drought-tough relative of the familiar prairie coneflower, green Mexican hat produces slender drooping rays of pale yellow to greenish-citron around a tall gray-green central cone, blooming through the hottest months of summer on wiry, well-branched stems. Native to caliche flats, limestone outcrops, and desert grasslands from Texas and New Mexico into northern Mexico, it thrives in lean, rocky, fast-draining soil and full sun with almost no supplemental water once established. Its low, spreading habit makes it a good edging or rock-garden choice where the larger Ratibida columnifera would be too coarse, and the blooms draw small native bees, skippers, and other short-tongued pollinators through late summer. Deadheading extends bloom, but plants also reseed modestly where soil is left open and undisturbed.

planting.note: Plant dormant tuberous roots or container divisions in fall into lean, well-drained prairie or glade soil; seed germination is slow and erratic without an extended cold, moist stratification period.

directions: One of the earliest prairie wildflowers to bloom, Carolina anemone sends up solitary, daisy-like flowers in shades of white, pale lavender, or pink with a bright yellow-green button center in early spring, often before the surrounding grasses have greened up. Found natively on dry limestone prairies, glades, and open rocky ground across the central and southern United States, it grows from small, knobby tuberous roots and goes fully dormant by early summer, so it pairs well with later-emerging warm-season grasses that fill the gap it leaves behind. The early, abundant pollen and nectar are valuable to queen bumblebees and other native bees emerging from overwintering before most other prairie plants have started blooming. Because it resents wet, heavy soil, it is best sited on a sunny, gritty slope or rock garden rather than typical garden loam.

planting.note: Set divisions or plugs in spring into lean, dry to average, well-drained soil in sun to light shade; established mats need almost no supplemental care and resent rich, wet ground.

directions: Howell's pussytoes forms low, spreading mats of narrow, felted, silver-green leaves that stay attractive through most of the growing season, sending up short flowering stems tipped with clusters of small, papery, cat's-toe-shaped flower heads in mid-spring. It is native to dry, open woodlands, sandy barrens, and rocky clearings across much of eastern and central North America, and like other pussytoes it is dioecious, with separate male and female colonies spreading slowly by stolons into a tight, weed-resistant groundcover. Early-season bees and small flies use the flowers for nectar and pollen when few other groundcovers are blooming, and the dense foliage also serves as a larval host for American Lady butterflies. It performs best in poor, gravelly, or sandy soils where more vigorous groundcovers would fail, making it a good choice for a dry meadow edge or gravel garden.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into well-drained, lean to average soil in partial shade to full sun; this species tolerates drier, more shaded sites than most other pussytoes.

directions: Parlin's pussytoes is a broad-leaved, mat-forming native of dry open woods, savannas, and old fields across the eastern and central United States, distinguished from other regional pussytoes by its comparatively large, spoon-shaped basal leaves with a felted silver-gray underside. Clusters of small, fuzzy, whitish-pink flower heads open atop short stalks in mid-spring, providing early forage for small native bees and flies at a time when little else is blooming in dry woodland understories. Like its relatives it is dioecious and spreads by short stolons to form a slowly expanding, drought-tolerant groundcover that suppresses weeds without needing mowing or irrigation. It is also a larval host plant for American Lady butterflies, whose caterpillars feed on the felted foliage.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto moist, average to rich soil in full sun to partial shade, or transplant spring-started plugs into consistently moist ground; seed needs light and cold, moist winter stratification to germinate well.

directions: Balsam ragwort is a cold-hardy native of calcareous fens, wet meadows, and rocky lakeshores across the northern United States and Canada, forming a basal rosette of smooth, spoon-shaped leaves topped in late spring by flat clusters of small, bright yellow daisy flowers on slender stems. It tolerates consistently moist to seasonally wet soils better than most Packera species and is well suited to rain gardens, pond margins, and wet prairie plantings where drainage is poor. The early yellow flowers are an important nectar and pollen source for small native bees, syrphid flies, and other early-season pollinators before most summer wildflowers have begun blooming. Plants slowly form loose colonies by short rhizomes and self-seed modestly in consistently damp, open ground.

planting.note: Sow seed outdoors in fall for natural cold stratification, or set out fall-planted, dormant nursery divisions into lean, well-drained soil; plants go summer-dormant and dislike wet soil once established.

directions: Upland larkspur is a compact, early-blooming wildflower of sagebrush steppe, dry montane meadows, and open pine woodlands across the intermountain West, producing loose spikes of rich blue-purple, spurred flowers in early to mid-spring on slender stems above deeply lobed, palmate leaves. Like other native larkspurs it completes most of its growth before summer drought sets in, then dies back to a dormant rootstock, so it is best combined with later-emerging bunchgrasses and summer-blooming perennials that can fill the space it vacates. The early nectar is an important resource for queen bumblebees, mason bees, and hummingbirds migrating north in spring. All plant parts are toxic if ingested, particularly to grazing livestock, so it should be sited away from pastures and kept out of reach of pets and children.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural stratification, or start indoors and transplant after the last frost, into average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this boneset tolerates drier soil than most Eupatorium species.

directions: Tall boneset is an upright native prairie and glade perennial with narrow, three-veined, willow-like leaves and dense, flat-topped clusters of small, fuzzy white flowers that open from late summer into fall. Unlike common boneset (Eupatorium perfoliatum), which prefers wet ground, this species thrives in lean, well-drained, even rocky or clay-heavy soils and is notably drought tolerant once established, making it a good fit for dry prairie restorations and unirrigated borders. The late-season blooms are a magnet for a wide range of small native bees, wasps, and migrating monarch butterflies at a time when many other nectar sources have finished for the year. Left standing through winter, the dried seed heads add texture to the garden and provide seed for songbirds.
